financial-assets-s2.title: Three places for $5,000 of savings
financial-assets-s2.html: Dana has saved $5,000 from a summer job and is weighing three choices: keep it in a checking account that pays almost no interest, buy a bond issued by a large company that pays a fixed 5% a year for ten years, or buy shares of stock in a young technology company whose price has swung up and down a lot.

nominal-real-rates-s2.html: A bank in the invented country of Arland lends Sam money for a car at a fixed nominal interest rate of 7% a year. When the loan is made, both Sam and the bank expect inflation of 3% a year. Over the next year, inflation turns out to be 6%.

items.q: In which year would the owner of the old bond most likely have to sell it for less than $1,000?
options: Year 2
Year 3
Year 4
Year 1

items.q: In Year 3, what most likely happens to the price of the old bond, and why?
options: It falls, because the interest rate fell
It rises, because it pays more than new bonds
It stays at $1,000, because the payment is fixed
It rises, because the bond pays more each year

items.q: In Year 2 a buyer pays $625 for the old bond. What interest rate does the buyer earn, as a percent of the price paid? (Divide the yearly payment by the price.)

mistakes.why: 5% is what the bond pays on its original $1,000 price. The buyer paid $625, so divide $50 by $625.
You divided the price by the payment. The rate is the payment over the price, times 100.

items.q: Across the four years, what does the table show about interest rates and the prices of existing bonds?
options: They move in the same direction
They are unrelated, since the payment is fixed
They move in opposite directions
Prices change but rates stay fixed

items.q: Which of Dana's choices is the most liquid?
options: The checking account
The company bond
The technology stock
The three are equally liquid

items.q: If Dana buys the company bond, what is she doing?
options: Buying part ownership of the company
Opening a deposit at the company
Paying the company for future goods
Lending money to the company

items.q: Why might the technology stock offer Dana a higher expected return than the checking account?
options: Its return is guaranteed by the company
It carries more risk, so buyers want more return
It is more liquid than a checking account
Its price can rise but not fall

items.q: A year after Dana buys the bond, interest rates on new company bonds rise to 7%. What happens to the market price of Dana's bond?
options: It rises, since rates on bonds went up
It stays the same, since her payment is fixed
It falls, since new bonds pay more
It falls, since the company now pays her less

items.q: What does liquidity measure?
options: How much interest an asset pays each year
How likely an asset is to lose value
How easily an asset becomes money without losing value
How many people own the asset

items.q: Which statement compares stocks and bonds correctly?
options: A stock is a loan to a firm; a bond is a share of ownership
A stock is a share of ownership; a bond is a loan to the issuer
Both are loans that pay a fixed interest rate
Both are shares of ownership in the issuer

items.q: Market interest rates fall sharply. What happens to people who already own bonds paying a fixed 6%?
options: They lose, because their payments are cut
They gain, because their bonds' prices rise
Nothing happens, because their rate is fixed
They gain, because their bonds now pay more interest

items.q: A company sells new bonds to pay for a new factory. In economic terms, what is the company doing?
options: Borrowing from the people who buy the bonds
Selling ownership shares to new investors
Lending money to the bond buyers
Saving part of its profit for later

items.q: Why is an interest rate called the price of borrowing?
options: It is the fee a bank charges to open an account
It is what a borrower pays to use someone else's money for a year, as a percent
It is the total amount a borrower repays at the end
It is the price of the goods bought with the loan

items.q: Which of these are financial assets? Select all that apply.
options: Shares of stock in a company
A bond issued by a city government
A delivery truck a bakery owns
A meal eaten at a restaurant

items.q: A bond pays $60 of interest a year. Hana buys it for $1,200. What interest rate does she earn on what she paid, in percent?

mistakes.why: You divided the price by the payment. Put the yearly payment on top: $60 / $1,200, times 100.
A 6% rate would be $60 on a $1,000 price. Hana paid $1,200, so she earns less: divide by $1,200.

items.q: Put the links in order, from a rise in market interest rates to the price of an existing bond.
options: Market interest rates rise
New bonds offer higher interest payments than the existing bond
Fewer buyers want the existing bond at its old price
The price of the existing bond falls until its yield matches the market rate

items.q: Make it specific: explain what a fall in market interest rates does to the price of an existing bond.

specific.frame: Market interest rates fall, so new bonds pay ___ than the existing bond; buyers ___ the existing bond, and its price ___.
specific.model: When market interest rates fall, new bonds pay less than the existing bond, so more buyers want the existing bond and its price rises, because its fixed payment now beats what new bonds offer.

link.label: What new bonds pay
options: less
more

why.1: Lower market rates mean new bonds pay less, not more.

change.label: What buyers do
options: want more of
want less of

why.1: The existing bond now pays more than new ones, so it is more attractive, not less.

price.label: The bond price
options: rises
falls

why.1: Bond prices move opposite to interest rates: rates fall, prices rise.

items.q: Which asset is the least liquid?
options: A $20 bill in a wallet
A checking account balance
A savings account balance
A rental house

items.q: What is the real interest rate on Loan C, in percent?

mistakes.why: You added the expected inflation rate. Inflation eats into what the lender gains, so subtract it: 9% - 3%.
You divided. The real rate is a difference: the nominal rate minus the expected inflation rate.

items.q: Which loan has a negative real interest rate?
options: Loan A
Loan B
Loan C
Loan D

items.q: Which loan gives its lender the largest expected gain in buying power?
options: Loan A, at 4% real
Loan D, since its two rates match
Loan B, with the lowest inflation risk
Loan C, at 6% real

items.q: What does Loan D's real interest rate tell its lender?
options: The lender expects to lose money in dollars
The lender expects no gain in buying power
The lender expects to earn 5% more buying power
The loan pays no interest in dollars

items.q: What real interest rate did the bank actually earn over the year, in percent?

mistakes.why: 4% is the real rate the bank expected. Over the year inflation was 6%, so the real rate earned was 7% - 6%.
Inflation is subtracted from the nominal rate, not added: 7% - 6%.

items.q: Who gained from the surprise in inflation, and why?
options: The bank, because prices rose faster
Sam, because his real rate fell
Neither, because the nominal rate stayed at 7%
Both, because incomes rose with prices

items.q: If lenders in Arland now expect inflation to stay at 6%, what most likely happens to the nominal rates they charge on new car loans?
options: They rise, to keep the real rate lenders want
They fall, because borrowers are gaining
They stay at 7%, because the real rate fell
They fall to the inflation rate of 6%

items.q: Which loan term would have protected the bank from this surprise?
options: A longer repayment period
A lower fixed nominal rate
A smaller down payment from Sam
A nominal rate that adjusts with inflation

items.q: What is a nominal interest rate?
options: The rate stated on a loan, in dollars
The rate after the expected inflation rate is subtracted
The rate a central authority sets for banks
The interest rate measured in goods instead of dollars

items.q: Which formula gives the real interest rate?
options: Nominal rate plus the expected inflation rate
Nominal rate divided by the expected inflation rate
Nominal rate minus the expected inflation rate
Expected inflation rate minus the nominal rate

items.q: A savings bond pays a nominal interest rate of 5%, and savers expect 2% inflation. What is the expected real interest rate, in percent?

mistakes.why: You added the expected inflation rate. Subtract it: 5% - 2%.
You divided. The real rate is the nominal rate minus the expected inflation rate.

items.q: A lender wants a real interest rate of 2% and expects inflation of 4%. What nominal interest rate should it charge, in percent?

mistakes.why: You subtracted. To find the nominal rate, add the expected inflation rate to the real rate the lender wants.
2% is the real rate the lender wants. The nominal rate adds the 4% expected inflation rate.

items.q: Prices fall by 2% over a year, though everyone expected them to rise by 2%. A firm repays a loan at a fixed 5% nominal rate. How is the firm affected?
options: It gains, because prices fell
It is not affected, because its rate was fixed
It loses, because its real rate rose
It loses, because its nominal rate rose

items.q: Inflation turns out much higher than expected. Which of these are hurt? Select all that apply.
options: A bank holding many fixed-rate home loans
A family repaying a fixed-rate home loan
A saver who owns a fixed-rate bond
A firm repaying a fixed-rate business loan

items.q: Why do economists say a firm deciding whether to borrow for new equipment cares about the real interest rate?
options: The real rate is the rate written on the loan
Lenders ignore inflation when they set rates
The real rate is set by the government each year
It measures the true cost of borrowing in buying power

items.q: Make it specific: explain who gains when inflation turns out higher than expected on a fixed-rate loan.

specific.frame: Inflation turns out higher than expected, so the real interest rate on the loan is ___ than agreed; the ___ gains, because the dollars repaid buy ___.
specific.model: Inflation turned out higher than expected, so the real interest rate on the loan is lower than agreed, which means the borrower gains because the dollars repaid buy less than the lender expected.

rate.label: The real rate
options: lower
higher

why.1: Real rate = nominal - inflation. More inflation with the same nominal rate means a lower real rate.

claim.label: Who gains
options: borrower
lender

why.1: The lender is repaid in dollars worth less than planned, so the lender loses.

change.label: What the repaid dollars buy
options: less than expected
more than expected

why.1: Higher inflation means each dollar buys less, not more.

items.q: Put the steps in order to find a real interest rate.
options: Read the nominal interest rate on the loan
Find the expected inflation rate for the same period
Subtract the expected inflation rate from the nominal rate
State the result as the gain in buying power, in percent

items.q: Using the table, what is M1 in Tolvia, in billions of dollars?

mistakes.why: That is M2. Time deposits and money market funds are near-money, counted in M2 but not M1.
A credit card limit is a promise to lend, not money you hold, so it is not counted.

items.q: Using the table, what is M2 in Tolvia, in billions of dollars?

mistakes.why: M2 includes M1. Add currency and checkable deposits to the time deposits and money market funds.
Stock is a financial asset but not money; it has to be sold for money first.
Unused credit is not money anyone holds. Leave the credit card limits out.

items.q: Which asset in the table is counted in M2 but not in M1?
options: Currency held by the public
Checkable deposits
Small time deposits
Shares of stock

options: Their total is too large to count
They have to be sold for money before they can be spent
Their prices are set by the government
They earn no return for their owners

items.q: Prices in a country rise 40% in one year. Which function of its money is hurt the most?

items.q: Why is a credit card not counted as money?

items.q: Lee deposits $200 of cash into his checking account. What happens to M1 right away?

It falls by $200
It stays the same

items.q: What gives fiat money, such as a modern dollar bill, its value?

The paper and ink it is printed with

options: Coins and paper currency held by the public
A $5,000 certificate of deposit
A checking account balance

items.q: How much must the Bank of Tarn hold as required reserves, in dollars?

mistakes.why: You applied the ratio to reserves. The requirement is a share of deposits: $200,000 x 0.2.
160,000 is the part of deposits the bank does not have to hold. Required reserves are $200,000 x 0.2.

items.q: What are the Bank of Tarn's excess reserves, in dollars?

mistakes.why: 50,000 is all of its reserves. Subtract the $40,000 it is required to hold.
40,000 is the required part. Excess reserves are what is left: $50,000 - $40,000.

items.q: What is the most the Bank of Tarn can lend right now, in dollars?

mistakes.why: 50,000 is the most the whole banking system can create. One bank can lend only its own excess reserves.
150,000 is the loans it has already made. New lending is limited to its excess reserves.

items.q: If the Bank of Tarn lends all of its excess reserves, what is the most the money supply can increase across the whole banking system, in dollars?

mistakes.why: 10,000 is the first loan. Each loan is redeposited and partly lent again, so multiply by 1 / 0.2 = 5.
You multiplied by the ratio. The money multiplier is 1 / 0.2 = 5.
Use excess reserves, not total reserves: the required $40,000 cannot be lent.

items.q: How much do Zell First Bank's excess reserves rise because of the deposit, in dollars?

mistakes.why: The whole deposit becomes reserves, but 10% of it, $500, is required. Excess reserves rise by $4,500.
500 is the required part. Excess reserves are the rest: $5,000 - $500.

items.q: What happens to the money supply (M1) at the moment Jordan makes the deposit?
options: It rises by $5,000
It does not change
It falls by $5,000
It rises by $50,000

items.q: What is the most the money supply of Zell can increase as a result of Jordan's deposit, in dollars?

mistakes.why: You multiplied the whole deposit. It was already money (as cash), so only the excess reserves, $4,500, create new money.
4,500 is the first new loan. Each loan is redeposited and lent again, so multiply by 1 / 0.1 = 10.

items.q: Suppose instead that Zell's banks keep some excess reserves and people hold some of their loans as cash. How does the money supply change compare with your answer to the last question?
options: It is larger, because more cash is in circulation
It is the same, because the multiplier depends on the ratio
It is smaller, because less is lent at each round
It is zero, because no loans are made

items.q: What is fractional reserve banking?
options: Banks keep part of their deposits as reserves and lend out the rest
Banks hold 100% of deposits as reserves
Banks lend just the money their owners put in
Banks hold a fraction of their loans as cash for customers

items.q: The required reserve ratio is 0.25. What is the money multiplier?

mistakes.why: 0.25 is the ratio itself. The multiplier is 1 divided by the ratio.
You used 25 (the percent) instead of 1 / 0.25. Write the ratio as a decimal: 1 / 0.25 = 4.
You used 1 - 0.25. The money multiplier is 1 divided by the required reserve ratio, not by the share lent out.

items.q: The central bank raises the required reserve ratio from 0.1 to 0.2. What happens to the money multiplier?
options: It doubles from 10 to 20
It falls from 10 to 5
It rises from 5 to 10
It stays at 10, since deposits are unchanged

items.q: A bank lends $8,000 to a customer by adding it to her checking account. What happens to the money supply right away?
options: It is unchanged, because the bank lent its own money
It falls by $8,000, because the bank's reserves fall
It rises by $8,000
It rises by $80,000

items.q: On a commercial bank's balance sheet, which of these is a liability?
options: Its customers' checkable deposits
The loans it has made
Its reserves at the central bank
The government bonds it holds

items.q: The required reserve ratio is 0.1. A customer withdraws $1,000 in cash from her checking account. How do the bank's excess reserves change?
options: They fall by $1,000
They fall by $100
They fall by $900

items.q: Which of these are assets of a commercial bank? Select all that apply.
options: Reserves held in its vault and at the central bank
Loans it has made to households and firms
Checkable deposits of its customers
Its owners' equity

items.q: Put the links in order, from new excess reserves to a larger money supply.
options: A bank has new excess reserves
It lends them, creating a new checkable deposit
The borrower spends the money, and the seller deposits it in another bank
That bank keeps the required share and lends its new excess reserves

items.q: Make it specific: explain how a bank with excess reserves can increase the money supply.

specific.frame: The bank ___ its excess reserves, which creates new ___; when that money is redeposited, other banks lend again, so the money supply ___ by up to excess reserves times ___.
specific.model: The bank lends its excess reserves, which creates new checkable deposits; because the borrowed money is spent and redeposited, other banks lend again, so the money supply increases by up to excess reserves times the money multiplier.

tool.label: What the bank does
options: lends
holds

why.1: Reserves held in the vault create no new money; lending does.

link.label: What lending creates
options: checkable deposits
required reserves

why.1: Lending creates deposits for the borrower; required reserves are what banks must hold back.

direction.label: The money supply
options: increases
decreases

why.1: New loans add deposits, so the money supply rises.

multiplier.label: The multiplier
options: 1 / required reserve ratio
the required reserve ratio

why.1: Multiplying by the ratio shrinks the amount; the money multiplier is 1 divided by the ratio.

items.q: In the United States, which institution sets the reserve requirement for banks?
options: Congress, in the yearly budget
The Federal Reserve, the central bank
Each commercial bank, for itself
The Department of the Treasury

falls

items.q: On the money market graph, show the effect of the central bank's bond sale and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: a central bank sale of bonds

slips.MD: A bond sale changes how much money exists, the money supply. It does not change how much money people want to hold at each rate.

items.q: After the bond sale, what happens to Pell's price level and real output in the short run?
options: Both fall
Both rise
The price level falls and real output rises
Neither changes, because the money supply is not part of AD

items.q: What happens to the prices of existing bonds in Pell after the central bank sells bonds?
options: They rise, because bonds are in demand
They fall, as interest rates rise
They do not change, because bonds are not money
They rise, because interest rates rise

items.q: In which year did the central bank tighten (contract) monetary policy?
options: Year 2
Year 3
Year 4
Year 1

items.q: Reserves rose by $300 billion in Year 2, yet the federal funds rate did not change. Why?
options: Banks were required to hold the new reserves
The new reserves were too small to count
Reserve supply was in the flat part of reserve demand
The central bank sold bonds to cancel them out

items.q: After the change in Year 3, what most likely happens to the interest rates banks charge on new car loans and mortgages?
options: They rise
They fall
They stay the same, since reserves did not change
They fall at first, then rise

items.q: The data show the federal funds rate trading just below the interest on reserve balances each year. What does that tell you about the framework?
options: Reserves are limited, so the money supply sets the rate
Reserves are ample, so administered rates set the rate
Banks are short of reserves and borrow at the discount rate
The reserve requirement sets the rate

items.q: Label the axes and the curves of the reserve market graph (ample reserves).
The central bank operates with ample reserves and wants to fight inflation. It raises the interest rate it pays on reserve balances. Shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: a rise in the interest rate on reserve balances

slips.RS: With ample reserves, moving reserve supply along the flat part does not change the rate. The central bank raises its administered rate, which moves the flat part of reserve demand up.

items.q: With ample reserves, the central bank buys bonds and adds reserves, but leaves its administered rates unchanged. Show the effect on the reserve market and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: a central bank purchase of bonds that adds reserves

slips.RD: Reserve demand moves only when the administered rates change, and the question says they did not. Buying bonds adds reserves: the supply curve.

items.q: A central bank that operates with limited reserves buys government bonds. On the money market graph, shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: a central bank purchase of bonds

slips.MD: Buying bonds changes how much money exists, the money supply, not how much money people want at each rate.

items.q: A central bank that operates with limited reserves buys $20 million of government bonds from commercial banks. The required reserve ratio is 0.2. What is the most the money supply can increase, in millions of dollars?

mistakes.why: 20 is the first round: the new reserves. Banks lend them and the loans are redeposited, so multiply by 1 / 0.2 = 5.
You multiplied by the ratio. The money multiplier is 1 / 0.2 = 5.
No deposit was added, so nothing is held back as required reserves: the full $20 million is excess.

items.q: A central bank that operates with limited reserves lowers the discount rate. What happens to the money supply and interest rates?
options: The money supply falls and interest rates rise
The money supply rises and interest rates fall
The money supply rises and interest rates rise
Neither changes, since the discount rate is a fee

items.q: Which of these are expansionary monetary policy actions? Select all that apply.
options: With limited reserves, buying government bonds
With ample reserves, lowering the interest rate on reserve balances
With limited reserves, raising the required reserve ratio
With ample reserves, raising the overnight reverse repurchase rate

items.q: What is the federal funds rate?
options: The rate the government pays on its bonds
The rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves
The rate banks charge their best business customers
The rate of inflation the central bank aims for

items.q: With ample reserves, what is the central bank's main tool for moving the policy rate?
options: Changing the required reserve ratio
Buying and selling bonds to shift reserve supply
Setting its administered rates, mainly interest on reserve balances
Changing taxes and government spending

items.q: A central bank with ample reserves fights a recession. Put the links in order.
options: The central bank lowers its administered rates
The policy rate (federal funds rate) falls
Other interest rates, such as loan and mortgage rates, fall
Investment and interest-sensitive consumption rise
Aggregate demand shifts right, so real output rises and unemployment falls

items.q: Make it specific: a central bank with ample reserves faces an inflationary gap. Build the chain from its action to the price level.

specific.frame: The central bank ___ the interest rate on reserve balances, so the policy rate ___; borrowing costs rise, so investment ___; aggregate demand shifts ___, and the price level ___.
specific.model: The central bank raises the interest rate on reserve balances, so the policy rate rises; because borrowing costs rise, investment decreases, aggregate demand shifts left, and the price level decreases.

tool.label: The action
options: raises
lowers

why.1: Lowering the administered rate is expansionary; an inflationary gap calls for a higher rate.

rate.label: The policy rate
options: rises
falls

why.1: The policy rate follows the administered rate up.

spending.label: Investment
options: falls
rises

why.1: Higher borrowing costs make fewer projects worth doing.

direction.label: AD shifts
options: left
right

why.1: Less investment means less spending at every price level: a shift left.

price.label: The price level
options: falls
rises

why.1: A leftward AD shift lowers the price level.
